translations: After three days, the first genuine cheers erupted from the foot of the mountain. But the cheers only reached halfway before being pushed back by the remaining seven days. The people finally understood that disaster wasn't just a hot stone that could be moved out of the way; it was like seven drums still drumming away, still pounding away at their heads. A young man supported his elderly mother as they stepped into the shade, but the shade was so small it only covered half of one foot, so he pulled his foot back to let his mother stand further. Aman saw this and paused, erasing the witty remark he had written and simply writing: "Life is suffering, even a small shadow is precious."

Hou Yi didn't turn around. He could hear the cheers and the fear hidden within them. He carefully asked the wind beside him, "Do you still have the strength?" The wind, having been scorched by ten days of heat, had lost its spirit and only blew his hair slightly. Aman heard this and couldn't help but chime in, "If the wind had the strength, it would have blown me down the mountain to cool off earlier." But he quickly added, "Of course, it's best not to blow, as I still haven't finished writing." Hou Yi was distracted by Aman's joke and his shoulders relaxed for a moment, but he quickly regained his composure. He shot the fourth arrow at the fourth day. After the first three days fell, the remaining sun seemed to finally know fear, its flames flickering wildly, but the heat waves grew even more intense, as if it wanted to press people back into the pot before it left. Hou Yi closed his eyes, listened to the wind, and shot the fourth arrow from his fingers, piercing through a fold of the turbulent flames. The fourth day was pierced, and the light scattered into a million red scales, falling behind a distant mountain. Aman counted along, writing "four" when his pen slipped, and he quickly pressed it with his sleeve, "Don't run around, you're just a number, not the one being shot."

The flames from the fourth day swept over the mountain slope, and the grass ropes tied earlier were snapped by the hot wind, making a loud snapping sound. The people guarding the mountain path immediately crouched down, using stones to press down the knots, so the ropes wouldn't swing out to the steep slope. A child mimicked the adults, hugging a stone and almost flattening himself. When the wind passed, he looked up with a face full of ash, asking seriously, "Did I press it down?" The adult looked at the stone, which was still and hadn't moved, and then at the child's two thin arms, "You pressed it down, at least you didn't fly away."

The child thought this was a reasonable answer and got up, wanting to find an even bigger stone. Aman called out from across the mountain slope, "Don't move it! If you roll down with the stone, I'll have to rewrite you." The child immediately hid his hands behind his back, as if the stone hadn't been his to begin with. Hou Yi didn't turn around, but he raised his left hand, signaling everyone to stay in the leeward position. He himself moved to a rocky outcropping, where there was no rope to hold onto, and rocks continued to fall from the ground.

The fifth arrow couldn't be shot from its original position. The fire clouds from the fourth day were rolling over from the west, and if shot directly into the turbulent flow, the arrow's tail would veer off course. Hou Yi knelt down and picked up three pebbles, throwing them in different directions. The first one fell straight down, the second one was blown back to his feet, and the third one flew off to the east at an angle. Aman understood and wrote "wind blowing east," but when he looked at the word, he saw that he had drawn it like a crawling insect. He glanced at Hou Yi and then at the word, quietly adding two legs, "Now it at least knows which way to crawl."

Hou Yi moved seven steps east along the rocky outcropping, each step waiting for the falling rocks to stop rolling before he stepped down. When he drew his bow again, the laughter from below had stopped. The people held their breath, shielding the ropes, and the child also covered his mouth, peeking through the gaps. The earlier jokes hadn't made anyone forget the danger; instead, they had helped everyone find their correct position. Hou Yi listened as the wind evenly swept past the arrow's feathers, and only then did he string the fifth arrow.

The child beside him was holding his laughter so tightly that he let out a hiccup, and Aman said sternly, "Be serious, if I make a mistake in counting, the people in the future will have to endure an extra day of heat."

The fifth arrow shot down the fifth day. Hou Yi lowered his bow arm and let out a long breath. His shadow on the rock was stretched out extremely short, as if it too was reluctant to stay in the heat. The fifth day hung in the middle of the sky, with the light at its strongest, piercing the eyes of the onlookers. Hou Yi suddenly took a step to the left, using the mountain ridge to stabilize the arrow's tail, and the arrow light flew up, like an eagle that refused to close its eyes. When the fifth day was shot down, people at the well's edge cried out in shock, and someone even felt a hint of moisture on the well's wall. Aman quickly jotted it down and whispered, "The fifth day fell, and the well took a breath. I want to breathe too, but I'm still waiting in line."
